A lecture video uses each slide's speaker notes as its script, word for word.
Notes written to prompt you in a live class often sound wrong when a voice
reads them out to someone watching alone. This guide covers how to write
notes for the ear, and how lecturecast reads them.

## Write for someone listening

A listener cannot reread a sentence or glance back at a paragraph. Guides to
voice-over and broadcast writing agree on a few rules:

- **Write the way you talk.** Use contractions and everyday words. Drop
  written connectives such as "thus" and "moreover".
- **One idea per sentence.** If a sentence carries two ideas, split it. Vary
  the length so the narration does not sound clipped.
- **Picture one listener.** Talk to a single student, not to a room.
- **Say symbols and abbreviations in full.** Write "for example" rather than
  "e.g.", "percent" rather than "%", and "A D one" rather than "AD₁". Voice
  models guess at symbols, and each provider guesses differently.
- **Leave web addresses on the slide.** Name the page in the narration and
  put the link where students can click it.
- **Read it aloud.** Rewrite any sentence that makes you stumble or run out of
  breath.

## Leave the live room behind

Notes written for class assume a room: "so the room can see", "click the
button", "turn to your neighbor". In the video nobody is in the room, and the
charts play by themselves. Describe what happens instead: "Watch what happens
when aggregate demand falls."

## Show, don't just tell

A video holds attention when the picture moves with the voice. Narrate every
slide, so there is no dead air: give section slides a one-sentence
transition, and give the title slide a short intro with
`title-slide-attributes: data-notes:` in the deck's YAML. Keep the agenda
slide short. On a slide you explain at length, reveal the points one at a
time as you reach them, or play a chart step, so the screen changes at
least every half minute. When one button plays a whole multi-step story,
give each step its own button that jumps to that step, and quote it as you
explain the step, so the viewer sees the whole and then each part.

## How lecturecast reads the notes

- **One slide, one segment.** The notes for a slide are voiced while that
  slide is on screen.
- **Fragments.** On a slide with fragments, put a line holding only `---`
  before each fragment's narration. The notes then need one part more than
  the slide has fragments: the first part plays before any fragment appears.
- **Animated charts.** A phrase in quotes that matches a button label on the
  slide, such as "AD falls", plays that button when the narration reaches it.
  Only the first mention on a slide plays. A quoted phrase that matches no
  button is read as ordinary text.
- **Silent slides.** A slide with no notes stops the build, unless it is marked
  silent with a length in seconds, either with `data-silent` on the slide or
  under `video: silent:` in `lecturecast.yml`.

`lecture_script()` shows every word as it will be voiced.

## Checking the notes

`lint_notes()` reads the rendered deck and lists what a listener is likely to
stumble on. It changes nothing; edit the notes in the deck's source and render
again.

```{r}
library(lecturecast)
issues <- lint_notes("slides/keynesian_slides.html")
```

It reports:

| Issue | Examples |
|---|---|
| symbol | `%`, `&`, `=`, arrows, subscripts, `and/or` |
| abbreviation | e.g., i.e., etc., vs. |
| link | `https://`, `www.` |
| acronym | SRAS, AD, MPC, SE, CI, OLS and other economics and statistics abbreviations, with the words to say |
| room | "the room", "in class", "click", "your neighbor" |
| long sentence | more than `max_words` words (30 by default) |
| dead air | a slide with nothing said, including the title slide |
| animation not cued | a chart button the notes never quote, so it never plays |
| static slide | narration running longer than `max_still` seconds (30 by default) with nothing changing on screen |
| static after animation | narration walking through an animation's steps after it has finished, while the chart sits at its end |

The result is a data frame with the slide, the sentence and advice for each
issue, so it can be filtered or saved:

```{r}
subset(issues, issue == "room")
```

Not every flag needs a change. Some voices read a symbol well, and some long
sentences flow well aloud. Each flag marks a place worth listening to again.

## With an AI assistant

lecturecast is meant to be used alongside an AI assistant. The package ships
a skill, `lecture-video`, in `system.file("skills", package = "lecturecast")`.
It runs `lint_notes()`, drafts a before and after for each flagged sentence
for you to approve, applies only what you approve to the deck's source, and
previews the changed slides with `build_video(slides = ...)`. Its table of
spoken forms (SRAS as "short-run aggregate supply", and so on) is the same
list `lint_notes()` checks.
